10.1016_j.envpol.2026.128675: Microplastic contamination of tropical mangrove fisheries remains poorly quantified, and polymer-specific ecological and dietary risks are rarely integrated for West African estuaries. This study assessed microplastic abundance, polymer composition, ecological risk, and human dietary exposure in commercially important finfish and crustacean species from the Escravos Estuary, Nigeria, using stereomicroscopy, FTIR identification, toxicity-weighted indices, and ingestion-based exposure modelling. Microplastics were detected in all taxa, with a mean abundance of 4.30 ± 0.76 particles g -1 . Surface water averaged 20.5 ± 0.7 particles L -1 (n = 2 duplicate samples), and polymer and shape profiles broadly co-occurred between water and biota. Filaments (35%) and fibres (24%) dominated, while transparent and blue particles were most common, suggesting inputs from wastewater, fishing gear, and packaging materials, with possible pigment bleaching under tropical solar exposure. Detected polymers included polyvinyl alcohol, polyacrylamides, chlorosulfonated polyethylene, polystyrene, polymethyl methacrylate, and polyamides. Toxicity-weighted indices were calculated only for polymers with published hazard scores. The mean polymer ecological risk index for water indicated Class IV (7.4 × 10 3 ), and assemblage-level BALI exceeded one. Plastic Estimated Daily Intake values, derived from gastrointestinal concentrations as conservative upper-bound estimates, ranged from 1.35–2.24 particles kg -1 bw day -1 for adults and 6.31–13.59 particles kg -1 bw day -1 for children, reflecting gastrointestinal rather than edible-tissue exposure. Toxicity-weighted risk was more strongly associated with polymer hazard than particle abundance. Despite limited spatial replication from a single wet-season survey (May 2025), the findings support polymer-informed frameworks for environmental and human exposure assessment in tropical mangrove ecosystems.
10.1016_j.snr.2026.100454: Periodontitis is a widespread inflammatory oral disease that requires rapid and accurate diagnosis in order to achieve better therapeutic outcomes. For this purpose, biosensors embedded in microfluidics offer great potential for the development of rapid tests. This study reports on the development of microfluidic chips for enzyme-based nucleic acid detection using electrochemical (EC) and chemiluminescent (CL) detection. The chips were tested using DNA standards specific to the parameter of total germ load (TGL), Prevotella intermedia (Pi), Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans (Aa), Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg), Treponema denticola (Td), and Tannerella forsythia (Tf). Both, EC and CL detection, exhibited dynamic ranges of 0.01–25 nM. However, CL showed higher sensitivity and reproducibility (LOD-span of 12–120 pM) than EC (LOD-span of 2 pM–1.2 nM), with the best LODs achieved for TGL (0.05 nM CL, 0.03 nM EC) and Pg (0.01 nM CL, 0.02 nM EC). Cell detection based on ribosomal RNA analysis was evaluated using Escherichia coli cells as TGL parameter and Pi cells, applying ionic liquid–based lysis at room temperature. Here, EC detection showed improved sensitivities (LODE.coli 3.44×104 cells/µL and LODPi 5.6×10⁵ cells/µL) compared to CL (LODE.coli 9.7×104 cells/µL and LODPi 1.03×106 cells/µL). Overall, the findings underscore the chip’s potential as a sensitive, versatile platform for point-of-care diagnostics in periodontology.
